name: Pumpkin seed oil

lead: Pumpkin seed oil, pressed from Cucurbita pepo seeds, is taken as an oral supplement or applied to the scalp by people hoping to slow or reverse male pattern hair loss and get thicker hair.

It is rich in unsaturated fatty acids, phytosterols and tocopherols, and phytosterols may weakly inhibit 5-alpha-reductase in laboratory studies. A 2014 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in men with androgenetic alopecia reported higher hair counts after 24 weeks, and a 2021 trial compared it with 5% minoxidil foam in women. Reviews describe these studies as small.

paras: It is usually taken as a daily capsule or oil, or used as a scalp product, often alongside approved treatments. Trial results were measured over about six months.
It is typically well tolerated, with occasional gastrointestinal upset or allergic reactions in people allergic to seeds. Product quality varies because it is sold as a food or supplement.

angle.text: Pumpkin seed oil is taken or applied for thicker scalp hair in male pattern hair loss. Its phytosterols may weakly reduce DHT activity at the follicle. A 2014 trial in men reported higher hair counts after 24 weeks, though studies are small.

lead: Pumpkin seed oil is a dark green to reddish culinary oil pressed from pumpkin seeds, associated especially with Styria in southeastern Austria and neighbouring parts of central and eastern Europe, and now also sold as an oral supplement and topical hair product [1][2]. It is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids and contains phytosterols, tocopherols and squalene [2][3].

In appearance communities it is discussed as a natural remedy for androgenetic alopecia. Human evidence is limited: a 2014 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in men with androgenetic alopecia examined oral pumpkin seed oil, and a 2021 randomised trial compared it with 5% minoxidil foam in women with female pattern hair loss [4][5]. Reviews of natural products and supplements for hair loss describe these studies as small and preliminary [6][7][8].
It is also studied for benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms and cardiovascular outcomes in postmenopausal women [9][10][11].

paras: The oil has an intense nutty flavour and is used as a salad dressing, on desserts such as ice cream, and in soups; Wikipedia notes that heating it for cooking is said to destroy its essential fatty acids [1]. Styrian oil is made by pressing roasted seeds of the hull-less Styrian oil pumpkin [1].

Oral and topical pumpkin seed oil is marketed for hair growth in androgenetic alopecia. Reviews list it among natural products with clinical data, alongside saw palmetto, caffeine, melatonin and rosemary oil [6][12][13].

Trials have examined pumpkin seed oil for benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms, compared against tamsulosin and prazosin [9][10], and for arterial function and blood pressure in postmenopausal women [11][14][15].

Male pattern hair loss: a 2014 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial studied oral pumpkin seed oil on hair growth in men with androgenetic alopecia [4][16]. The sources available here do not give the numerical results, and the report is a single small study without published independent replication.
Female pattern hair loss: a 2021 randomised comparative trial assigned 30 women to pumpkin seed oil and 30 to minoxidil 5% foam [5].

Reviews: a 2023 JAMA Dermatology systematic review of nutritional supplements for hair loss in people without known deficiency included 17 randomised trials and other studies [7]. A 2022 review of natural products for male androgenetic alopecia identified 11 clinical studies and stated that pumpkin seed oil, among others, might be considered [6]. A review of topical alternatives found studies mostly small, often of combined formulations, with limited sample size, lack of comparison with standard therapy and conflicts of interest [8]. Other reviews of herbal and complementary supplements are available [12][13][17].

Prostate: randomised trials compared pumpkin seed oil with tamsulosin and with prazosin in symptomatic BPH [9][10]. Cardiovascular: randomised trials in postmenopausal women examined arterial hemodynamics and stiffness [11][14][15].

The oil's phytosterols are proposed to weakly inhibit 5-alpha-reductase and its tocopherols and squalene to have antioxidant effects, though the mechanism in people is not established [3][6]. Grokipedia reports in vitro antioxidant and antimicrobial activity [2]. A comprehensive review addresses its composition, benefits and safety [3].

The comprehensive review of the oil as a functional food covers safety [3]. Allergic reactions in people sensitive to seeds are a general consideration for seed products, and reviews of natural hair products note that supplement quality varies [8].

According to Grokipedia, pumpkin seed records in Styria date to 1697, oil production to 1735, and a hull-less mutation of the Styrian oil pumpkin appeared around 1880; the oil was used in folk medicine for urinary and prostate complaints [2]. Grokipedia is AI-generated, so these dates are reported as stated there.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, pumpkin seed oil is discussed mainly as a natural option for hair loss, with users asking whether it is effective or "another cope" compared with approved treatments [18].
